t:
Section 503 of such Act (22 U.S.C. 1643b) is amended as follows:

    (1) 
After “the Government of Cuba” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “, or the Chinese Communist regime,”;
 
    (2) 
After “since January 1, 1959,” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “in the case of claims against the Government of Cuba, or since October 1, 1949, in the case of claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”;
 
    (3) 
After “within sixty days after the enactment of this title” insert “or sixty days after the enactment of the amendments made thereto with respect to claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”; and
 
    (4) 
After “carrying out its functions” insert “with respect to each respective claims program authorized,”.

fable.w: This section only makes technical amendments extending an existing claims program against Cuba to cover claims against the Chinese Communist regime. The tempting reading is that claims filed by outside parties count as participation, but filing a claim for compensation is like applying for a benefit, not being consulted on a federal decision. Nothing in the text creates a comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, or a right to sue.
fable.s: in the case of claims against the Government of Cuba, or since October 1, 1949, in the case of claims against the Chinese Communist regime,

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of textual amendments to an existing statute, specifically expanding the scope of a claims program to include the Chinese Communist regime. It does not establish any new process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards, or hearings. The text merely defines the entities and timeframes relevant to the claims program without involving external participation in decision-making.
qwen_block.s: Section 503 of such Act (22 U.S.C. 1643b) is amended as follows: (1) After “the Government of Cuba” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “, or the Chinese Communist regime,”; (2) After “since January 1, 1959,” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “in the case of claims against the Government of Cuba, or since October 1, 1949, in the case of claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”; (3) After “within sixty days after the enactment of this title” insert “or sixty days after the enactment of the amendments made thereto with respect to claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”; and (4) After “carrying out its functions” insert “with respect to each respective claims program authorized,”.

opus.w: The amendment extends an existing claims program so it also covers claims against the Chinese Communist regime, and it adjusts dates and deadlines. Submitting a claim for compensation is like applying for a benefit, which the definition excludes. It does not let outsiders help shape a federal decision. Nothing here requires consultation, hearings, comment periods or advisory bodies, and it does not give anyone a right to challenge a federal decision.
opus.s: After “the Government of Cuba” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “, or the Chinese Communist regime,”;
opus.b: 1. **The tempting reading:** This amendment deals with "claims" against foreign governments. That could look like outsiders formally objecting to or seeking review of a decision. It doesn't hold up against the definition. Section 503 of the International Claims Settlement Act covers the Foreign Claims Settlement Commission's work on claims by U.S. nationals against Cuba, and this amendment extends it to claims against the Chinese Communist regime. Filing such a claim is a request for compensation, much like an application for benefits. It is not a chance to shape a federal policy decision or to sue over one. The amendment only adds a second country, a cutoff date, and a filing deadline. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section consists entirely of textual amendments to an existing statute, expanding the scope of a claims program to include claims against the Chinese Communist regime and adjusting relevant dates. It does not establish any mechanism for outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) to consult with, comment on, or participate in the federal government's decision-making process. The changes are legislative directives, not participatory procedures.
qwen_chat.s: Section 503 of such Act (22 U.S.C. 1643b) is amended as follows: (1) After “the Government of Cuba” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “, or the Chinese Communist regime,”; (2) After “since January 1, 1959,” at each place it appears in subsections (a) and (b) thereof insert “in the case of claims against the Government of Cuba, or since October 1, 1949, in the case of claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”; (3) After “within sixty days after the enactment of this title” insert “or sixty days after the enactment of the amendments made thereto with respect to claims against the Chinese Communist regime,”; and (4) After “carrying out its functions” insert “with respect to each respective claims program authorized,”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that amending the scope of a claims program involves "participation" because it affects claimants (outsiders). However, the text itself only describes legislative amendments to dates and entities; it does not establish a process for outsiders to consult, comment, or participate in the decision-making. The definition requires the *section* to involve participation (e.g., a hearing, comment period, advisory board with outsiders). This section is purely definitional/amendatory regarding the scope of a program, not a procedural mechanism for outside input.
